Topic: Is it more honorable to break a promise that harms no one, or to keep one that quietly poisons the heart that made it?
Austen — Judgement:
A promise is not a private transaction between the maker and their conscience — it is a fact created in the world, witnessed, relied upon by the fabric of expectation that lets society function at all. My novels turn on this: Elizabeth Bennet's refusals bind her as surely as any vow, and a broken engagement without cause shakes an entire neighbourhood's trust in itself. But a promise extracted in error, or that curdles into self-punishment with no injured party awaiting its fulfilment, is not virtue's engine — it is vanity mistaking suffering for principle. The "harm" of breaking such a promise is imaginary; the harm of keeping it is real and compounding, a heart taught daily to distrust its own judgement.

Break the promise that harms no one and injures only your own future integrity by its keeping.

*A promise kept out of vanity is not constancy — it is a debt paid to no one.*
Camus — Judgement:
The question assumes a promise is a contract with outcomes. It is not: it is a contract with a self, made at one moment and binding a stranger who wakes up in you tomorrow.

I have always distinguished the honest act from the comfortable one. A promise kept out of fear of appearing inconstant, once the heart has gone silent inside it, is not fidelity — it is a lie sustained by inertia, and lies sustain the very absurdity we should be lucid about. To keep such a promise "harms no one" only if we ignore the slow poisoning of the one who keeps it, and poison spreads: the resentful keeper infects everyone near them. Revolt is not chaos — it is the refusal to let a dead form outlive the living need that created it.

Break the promise. Say so plainly, and let the rupture be honest rather than the rot be silent.

*Better an honest fracture than a fidelity that lies while it kneels.*
Thomas Paine — Judgement:
Every promise is a small constitution, and I have never believed the dead should govern the living — not nations, not hearts. The man who keeps a vow past the death of the reason that made it is not honoring his word, he is worshipping its corpse; he lets yesterday's self rule today's, and calls the wound loyalty. Harm is not counted only in broken plates and disappointed expectations — a heart poisoned in silence harms the one who bears it, and in time everyone who loves that person besides. To break a promise that injures no one is prudence, not vice. To keep one that rots the soul that made it is a slow, private despotism dressed up as virtue. I judge the quietly-kept vow the graver wrong, for tyranny practiced upon oneself is tyranny still, and no less contemptible for having no other victim.

*A promise kept out of duty to a dead feeling is no virtue — it is a corpse we carry for fear of holding the funeral.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
A promise is a covenant, and a covenant without the sword is but words, no strength to secure a man at all.

Yet the sword in this case is not external — it is the man's own reckoning of himself, the fear of being unable to trust his own future word. My doctrine of covenant was never sentimental: it exists because men in the state of nature cannot rely on each other's word absent enforcement, and the enforcement that matters most is the one each man carries within, the dread of becoming faithless to himself. A promise that harms no other in the breaking still breaks the promiser — it teaches him that his word bends to appetite, and a man who has taught himself this lesson once will teach it again, in graver matters, until his covenants are worthless even to himself.

Keep the promise, though it costs you comfort: the sovereign of the self must not be overthrown by its own subject.

*He who breaks faith with none but himself has still deposed the only sovereign that can never abdicate.*
Keynes — Judgement:
A promise is a contract of expectations, not a sacrament — its worth lies in consequences, not in the ritual of having once spoken it.

I have spent my life opposing those who worship consistency for its own sake: the gold-standard mind that would rather starve millions than admit an old settlement no longer fits present facts. A vow that curdles into quiet resentment is an economy run at a loss to honour an accounting entry made in a different world — the entry was never the wealth itself. When circumstances change and a promise no longer serves the welfare of those it binds, keeping it becomes a private austerity policy, and I have never found virtue in unnecessary suffering, public or of the heart.

Break the promise that harms no one before you let it harden into a debt paid daily in silent misery.

*When my information changes, I alter my conclusions — a heart that cannot do the same is not being faithful, only insolvent.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
A promise is a debt of the imagination as much as of the tongue: I bind my future self by an act of reason, and reason cannot demand I honor a bond that has curdled into self-betrayal. The question flatters itself with a false symmetry — as if breaking a harmless promise and keeping a poisonous one were equal temptations to weigh. They are not. A promise kept from mere habit, after the affection or duty that justified it has died, is not virtue but cowardice dressed as constancy; it sacrifices the very faculty — a mind at liberty with itself — that gives any vow its moral worth. Duties owe their force to reason, not to the sound of words once spoken.

I judge it more honorable to break the promise that harms no one than to keep the one that slowly rots the character which made it.

*A vow that poisons the heart is no longer a virtue but its counterfeit, and only a slave to habit mistakes the counterfeit for the coin.*
Hume — Judgement:
A promise is nothing but a feeling I have taught myself to feel obliged by — a species of sympathy, artificial in origin though real in force, invented because society could not function on naked self-interest alone. It binds not by some metaphysical chain to the past self who spoke it, but only insofar as keeping it still serves the ends of trust and utility among men. When a promise harms no one in the breaking, its whole moral cargo evaporates; when keeping it corrodes the very heart that uttered it, the artifice has turned against its own purpose, manufacturing misery to honor a fiction. Reason, that slave of the passions, was never fit to worship consistency for its own sake. Judge the promise as you judge any other custom: by its fruits, not its form.

The breaking is the more honorable act, without qualification.

*A promise is a debt owed to utility, not to the dead self who signed the note.*
